'''''Pinus bungeana''''' ({{zh|s=白皮松|p=báipísōng}}; [[Japanese language|Japanese]]: シロマツ; {{Korean|백송||baeksong}}), also known by the common names '''Bunge's pine''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PIBU2|taxon=Pinus bungeana|accessdate=4 October 2015}}</ref> '''lacebark pine''' and '''white-barked pine''', is a [[pine]] tree native to northeastern and central [[China]].<ref name="efloras">{{eFloras|2|200005327|Pinus bungeana |family=Pinaceae |first1=Liguo |last1=Fu |first2=Nan |last2=Li |first3=Thomas S. |last3=Elias |first4=Robert R. |last4=Mill |access-date=2018-08-16}}</ref><ref name="gymnobase">{{Gymnosperm Database |genus=Pinus |species=bungeana}}</ref>  It is a slow-growing [[tree]] that can grow to heights of {{convert|15|–|25|m|ft}} is frost hardy down to below {{convert|-26|°C|°F}}. Its smooth, grey-green [[bark (botany)|bark]] gradually sheds in round scales to reveal patches of pale yellow, which turn olive-brown, red and purple on exposure to light.
[[Image:Pinus_bungeana_Kew1.jpg|thumb|left|Lacebark pine at [[Kew Gardens]], London, England]]

== Description ==
The lacebark pine's trunk can grow either [[monopodial]], as a single growth upwards, or [[Sympodial branching|sympodial]], forked. Its crown is loosely shaped like a pyramid or umbrella. It has {{convert|5|–|10|cm|in}} long needles in groups of three. Each needles' cross-sections are shaped like a triangular semicircle. The lacebark pine produces [[Conifer cone|cones]] that turn yellowish brown as they mature and are roughly egg-shaped and {{convert|5|–|7|cm|in}} long. They contain seeds that are grey-brown, slightly egg-shaped, and {{convert|10|mm|in}} long.<ref name="efloras" />

[[Image:Pinus bungeana Kew2.jpg|thumb|left|Closeup of multiple stems]]

== Taxonomy ==
''P. bungeana'' is synonymous with the name ''Pinus excorticata'', attributed to Lindley and Gordon in [[William Dallimore]]'s ''Handbook of Coniferae and Ginkgoaceae''. Its name is derived from the surname "Bunge", as one of its early identifications was by botanist [[Alexander von Bunge]] in 1831 near [[Beijing]].

''P. bungeana'' is closely related to ''[[Pinus gerardiana]]'', another pine species with flaking bark, but ''P. bungeana'' has stiffer needles and smaller cones.<ref name=handbook>{{ cite book | last1=Dallimore | first1=William | author1-link=William Dallimore | last2=Jackson | first2=Albert Bruce | author2-link=Albert Bruce Jackson | year=1923 | chapter=Pinus |title=A handbook of Coniferae, including Ginkgoaceæ | edition=1 | location=New York | publisher=Longmans, Green & Co. | pages=375–377 | chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofconife00dall/page/374/mode/2up |doi=10.5962/bhl.title.15657 }}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Pinus bungeana'' is native to temperate forests in the mountains of China, but it is also widely cultivated as an [[ornamental tree]], especially for its metallic bark.<ref name="iucn status 13 November 2021" /> It grows in the provinces of [[Shanxi]], west [[Henan]], south [[Gansu]], south [[Hebei]], north [[Sichuan]], [[Shaanxi]], west [[Shandong]], and [[Hubei]]. It occurs in the wild on limestone rocks and south-facing slopes at relatively high elevations of {{convert|500|–|2150|m|ft}}, but has also been planted at lower elevations. In the northern portion of its range, it also occurs in [[acidic soil]]. As a light-demanding species, it usually grows in sites less suitable for other tree species.<ref name="iucn status 13 November 2021" />

It was introduced to [[England]] in 1843.<ref name="iucn status 13 November 2021" />
[[Image:Pinus bungeana Kew3.jpg|thumb|center|Closeup of bark]]

== Ecology ==
Pollination of the lacebark pine occurs in the months of April and May, while seeds mature in October and November of the second year.<ref name="efloras" />

== Uses ==
In China and Korea, the lacebark pine is traditionally planted near temples and cemeteries.<ref name="iucn status 13 November 2021" /> It is also grown as an ornamental tree in classical gardens seeking to imitate Chinese gardens, in which it symbolizes longevity. It can also be seen in botanic gardens and often grows with multiple stems.{{Citation needed|date=February 2023}}

The wood of the lacebark pine is not commercially used as timber, but it is used locally by populations in northeast China for construction, furniture, and transport structures like [[Pallet|pallets]]. The lacebark pine has edible seeds used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]] to provide relief for [[Respiratory system|respiratory]] ailments.<ref name="iucn status 13 November 2021" />

[[Image:Lacebark Pine bark and foliage at the BBG.jpg|left|thumb|Bark and foliage]]

==Cultural significance==
In 2009, ''P. bungeana'' was named the city tree of [[Baoji]], China.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.sina.com.cn/c/2009-04-26/033815528421s.shtml |title=海棠花成为宝鸡市市花 |trans-title=Asiatic apple flower becomes city flower of Baoji |author=张红平 |publisher=Sina Corporation |language=zh |date=2009-04-26 |access-date=2023-02-14}}</ref>
